claims.claim: The 1987 Brundtland Report defined sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.'

The report was 'Our Common Future,' produced by the UN World Commission on Environment and Development chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, published 1987 (UN document A/42/427), and led to the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.

The definition contains two key concepts: 'needs' (with overriding priority to the essential needs of the world's poor) and 'limitations' imposed by technology and social organization on the environment's ability to meet present and future needs.
The UN adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals in 2015 under the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with a 2030 target year, extending the sustainable-development framing globally.

The planetary-boundaries framework, proposed in 2009 by Rockstrom and colleagues, identifies nine earth-system processes defining a 'safe operating space for humanity'; a 2023 update in Science Advances found six of the nine transgressed, and a 2025 update reported ocean acidification as a seventh.

The U.S. EIA classifies renewable energy sources (solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, biomass) as replenished by nature and non-renewable sources (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium/nuclear) as finite stocks formed over geological time.

Garrett Hardin's 1968 'tragedy of the commons' describes self-interested overuse of a shared resource beyond its carrying capacity, degrading it for all; later work by Elinor Ostrom showed communities often govern common resources sustainably through institutions.

Weak sustainability assumes human-made capital can substitute for natural capital (total capital must not fall), while strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital is non-substitutable and must be preserved; the distinction is a genuine, ongoing debate.

That the climate is warming and human greenhouse-gas emissions are the dominant cause is established science; specific policy responses are genuinely contested. The lesson keeps these separate and adjudicates no policy.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many planetary boundaries are transgressed
positions: 2023 update (Richardson et al., Science Advances): six of nine transgressed
2025 update reported by the Stockholm Resilience Centre: seven, adding ocean acidification
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson cites the 2023 published figure as primary and notes the 2025 update, dating both. Figures are revised as science improves; presented as a scientific model of limits, not a fixed legal threshold.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether shared resources inevitably suffer a 'tragedy of the commons'
positions: Hardin (1968): individually rational overuse tends to destroy shared resources
Ostrom and later scholarship: communities frequently manage commons sustainably via rules and institutions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both presented: Hardin names the overshoot mechanism; Ostrom shows it is not inevitable. Neither treated as the whole story.

positions: Weak: natural capital is substitutable by human-made capital
Strong: critical natural capital is non-substitutable
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an unresolved analytical debate that explains why the concept is contested at the edges; the lesson adjudicates neither.
